items.location: Amendment P00004 (Standard Form 30), block 14 Description of Amendment
items.anchor_quote: The proposal period is hereby extended to 5:00 p.m. EDT, May 21, 2025.
items.summary: Amendment P00004 to solicitation 80NSSCFY25SBIRPhaseI (solicitation dated 1/08/2025 in block 9B) changes the NAICS 541713/541715 registration requirement from time of proposal submission to time of contract award, states that no acknowledgment is required, and extends the proposal period to 5:00 p.m. EDT on May 21, 2025. The SF-30 is digitally signed by Contracting Officer Charles "Chris" Bridges, dated 5/19/2025 (block 16C).

numbers.meaning: new proposal deadline (May 21, 2025, 5:00 p.m. EDT)
date amendment signed by Contracting Officer (5/19/2025)

items.scope_notes: Administrative/procurement information only; says nothing about fire detection science. Cover-page dates are needed to date the solicitation text (FY2025 Phase I).

items.location: Amendment P00004 page 2 of 3, change to Cover Page
items.anchor_quote: Proposal Package Due Date and Time changed,
items.summary: The amendment changes the cover-page proposal package due date from March 10, 2025 (5:00 p.m. ET) to May 21, 2025 (5:00 p.m. ET); it also moves the Help Desk question cut-off from March 3, 2025 to May 20, 2025 and replaces the protest contracting officer (Kenneth Albright to Charles Bridges, per page 3).

numbers.meaning: original due date (March 10, 2025)
amended due date (May 21, 2025)

items.scope_notes: Administrative change history of the solicitation; no technical content.

items.location: Section 1.2 Purpose and Priorities (printed page 2)
items.anchor_quote: NASA will release its FY 2025 Phase I SBIR solicitation on January 7, 2025.
items.summary: The solicitation body states that NASA would release the FY 2025 Phase I SBIR solicitation on January 7, 2025, with completed proposal packages due Wednesday, May 21, 2025, 5:00 p.m. Eastern (as amended). Note the SF-30 block 9B gives the solicitation date as 1/08/2025, one day later than the release date stated here.

numbers.meaning: stated release date of the solicitation (January 7, 2025)

items.scope_notes: Dating information. The one-day difference (Jan 7 vs 1/08/2025) is reported as printed; the extractor did not resolve it.

items.location: S15.03 subtopic header (PDF pp. 254-260; printed pp. 246-252)
items.anchor_quote: S15.03: Environmental Monitoring for Micro-G and Partial-G Experiments
items.summary: Subtopic S15.03 "Environmental Monitoring for Micro-G and Partial-G Experiments (SBIR)" (Science Mission Directorate, Biological and Physical Sciences division) is led by ARC with GRC as participating center; related subtopic pointers are S15.02 and S17.03. It spans PDF pages 254-260 and contains two scopes, listed as not in priority order: (1) Continuous Environmental Sensing to Monitor the Space-Built Environment and Its Microbiome (PDF pp. 254-257) and (2) Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research (PDF pp. 257-260).
items.scope_notes: This is the only subtopic in the FY2025 Phase I solicitation whose scope is spacecraft fire detection / smoke sensing (within this document). Lead/participating centers as printed: "Lead Center: ARC", "Participating Center(s): GRC".

items.location: S15.03 > Subtopic Introduction
items.anchor_quote: the spaceflight research environment is constrained by high launch costs, restricted amounts of crew time,
items.summary: The S15.03 introduction says that interpreting space experiments requires high-quality environmental measurements, ideally reference quality with high temporal and spatial resolution, but that spaceflight research is constrained by high launch costs, limited crew time and the need for tight physical packaging; technologies are therefore sought to measure and report environmental parameters of experiments in space.
items.scope_notes: General framing for both S15.03 scopes; not specific to smoke detectors.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 title (PDF pp. 257-260; printed pp. 249-252)
items.anchor_quote: Scope Title: Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research
items.summary: Scope 2 of S15.03, "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research", runs from PDF page 257 (scope description) through PDF page 260 (relevance and references), lead center ARC, participating center GRC. Expected TRL at completion 2 to 6; primary taxonomy TX 08 Sensors and Instruments / TX 08.3 In-Situ Instruments/Sensor; desired deliverables research, analysis and prototype.
items.scope_notes: Scope-level metadata. TRL/taxonomy details appear on PDF page 258.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description
items.anchor_quote: Material combustion in reduced gravity or microgravity differs compared to combustion in Earth gravity
items.summary: The scope describes a spacecraft fire as one of the most dangerous scenarios for a crewed mission and states that combustion in reduced gravity or microgravity differs from combustion in Earth gravity because buoyant flow is reduced or absent, which changes heat and mass transfer and thereby affects material ignitability and flame-spread rates.
items.scope_notes: Background physics statement for the scope; no specific test, material or detector data given.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description
items.anchor_quote: The influence of gravity on fundamental combustion physics must be determined for relevant materials
items.summary: The scope states that the effect of gravity on fundamental combustion physics still has to be determined for relevant materials in order to understand how a fire may start and/or spread in space.
items.scope_notes: Stated as an open need in the solicitation; no materials are named and no gravity levels are quantified.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description
items.anchor_quote: These experiments will require combustion product sensors that can operate autonomously with minimal power
items.summary: With NASA planning a return to the Moon, BPS targets fundamental combustion experiments for future lunar landers; these will need combustion product sensors that run autonomously with minimal power consumption and a small physical footprint. The scope says this need for science-enabling sensors aligns with the need for improved fire detection systems for future missions.
items.scope_notes: Applies to future lunar-lander combustion experiments and, by stated alignment, to future fire detection systems; no performance numbers given in this sentence.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description (sentence begins on PDF p. 257)
items.anchor_quote: selectively detect smoke at concentrations low enough and within relevant particle size ranges
items.summary: Technology improvements are needed so that smoke is selectively detected at sufficiently low concentrations and within the relevant particle size ranges for the detector to alarm in a potential slow-moving spacecraft fire scenario.
items.scope_notes: A stated requirement implying concern that current detection may not alarm early enough for slowly developing fires; the solicitation does NOT document a specific missed-alarm event, test or detector failure here. Do not recode as missed_alarm.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description
items.anchor_quote: do not rely on a priori knowledge of combustion product concentrations or properties
items.summary: Proposals should address combustion product monitoring (smoke particles, gases, or both) for both combustion experiments and fire detection systems, specifically sensing strategies that selectively detect smoke and/or work without prior knowledge of combustion product concentrations or properties such as smoke particle sizes or morphologies.
items.scope_notes: Applies to both science experiments and fire detection systems. Implies that current approaches depend on assumed smoke properties (see SoA items); no specific detector named in this sentence.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description
items.anchor_quote: should be suitable for applications in desired experimental and/or habitat atmospheres, including reduced pressures
items.summary: Sensors should run autonomously and continuously, be suitable for experimental and habitat atmospheres including reduced pressures and elevated O2 concentrations, and provide data in real time with little or no crew time for download and transfer.
items.scope_notes: Atmosphere conditions are qualitative in this scope (no O2 percentage or pressure value given). For numeric exploration-cabin values see the H3.13 items (8.2 psia, >33.7 vol% O2, up to 38 vol%), which belong to a different subtopic.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description > hardware requirements list
items.anchor_quote: Measurement of two or more parameters is highly desired.
items.summary: The hardware must measure at least one particulate-phase parameter relevant to fire detection and/or reduced-gravity combustion (examples: particle mass concentration, number concentration, size distribution, charge distribution); measuring two or more parameters is highly desired, complementary gas-phase measurements in parallel are allowed, and any parameter not on the list must be justified.
items.scope_notes: Requirement list for proposals; this is NASA stating a desired multi-parameter capability, not a test result.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description > hardware requirements list
items.anchor_quote: Capability of measuring aerosol concentrations over 1 mg/m3 is desired.
items.summary: The hardware should operate over a wide dynamic concentration range; the ability to measure aerosol concentrations above 1 mg/m3 is desired.

numbers.meaning: desired measurable aerosol mass concentration (capability over this value)

items.scope_notes: Desired upper concentration capability; no lower detection limit is specified in the text.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description > hardware requirements list
items.anchor_quote: Capability of measuring particles with diameters from 10 to 300 nm is highly desired.
items.summary: The hardware should measure aerosol concentrations over a broad size range; measuring particles with diameters from 10 to 300 nm is highly desired, and size distribution capability is desired.

numbers.meaning: lower end of highly desired particle diameter range
upper end of highly desired particle diameter range

items.scope_notes: Desired size coverage. Compare with the SoA statement (PDF p. 259) that light-scattering techniques do not detect particles smaller than ~300 nm; the solicitation itself juxtaposes these only implicitly.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description > hardware requirements list
items.anchor_quote: Target habitats for operation include the International Space Station (ISS), commercial low-Earth-orbit (LEO) destinations,
items.summary: The hardware should work across space-habitat environments (non-standard atmosphere composition, reduced pressure, different airflow rates and gravity levels); target habitats are the ISS, commercial LEO destinations, Gateway, a future lunar surface habitat, pressurized rovers, and vehicles in transit to the Moon or Mars.

conditions.gravity: microgravity (ISS, LEO, Gateway, transit) and lunar partial gravity (surface habitat, rovers)

items.scope_notes: Lists required operating environments qualitatively; no numeric airflow, pressure or gravity values are given.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Scope Description > hardware requirements list
items.anchor_quote: Have reasonable mass, volume, and power requirements in light of typical requirements for space habitats.
items.summary: The hardware should take continuous measurements at a cadence suited to the parameter, minimise crew time for operation and data transfer, and have reasonable mass, volume and power for space habitats.
items.scope_notes: No numeric mass/volume/power limits are specified for proposals.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Expected TRL / taxonomy
items.anchor_quote: Expected TRL or TRL Range at completion of the Project: 2 to 6
items.summary: Expected TRL range at completion of the project is 2 to 6; primary technology taxonomy TX 08 Sensors and Instruments, level 2 TX 08.3 In-Situ Instruments/Sensor; desired deliverables are research, analysis and prototype.

numbers.meaning: lower expected TRL at completion
upper expected TRL at completion

items.scope_notes: Programmatic metadata for the fire detection scope (scope 1 of S15.03 lists TRL 3 to 5 instead).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Desired Deliverables Description
items.anchor_quote: Concepts that can achieve flight demonstration on a suborbital flight or on the ISS
items.summary: Phase I should deliver a feasibility study with proof of concept and a path toward an in-orbit hardware demonstration, optionally bench-top prototype components, plus a preliminary business case; Phase II should deliver a preliminary design, concept of operations, an engineering development unit and test report, with concepts able to fly on a suborbital flight or the ISS during Phase II described as especially valuable.
items.scope_notes: Deliverable expectations; identical wording is also used for S15.03 scope 1 (PDF p. 256).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 1)
items.anchor_quote: they often are limited in their applicability across relevant aerosol size/concentration ranges
items.summary: Commercial aerosol measurement technologies, including smoke detectors, are widely available but were generally designed for terrestrial use. Surrogate aerosol measurements such as optical particle counters offer size, mass and cost benefits, yet they often cover only part of the relevant aerosol size/concentration ranges and/or need prior knowledge of analyte properties to operate and interpret data.
items.detector: optical particle counters (surrogate aerosol measurements); commercial smoke detectors
items.scope_notes: Generic statement about commercial/surrogate aerosol sensors (optical particle counters named as example); no specific test data or reference is cited in the text for this claim.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 1)
items.anchor_quote: where particle properties and concentrations may not be fully known.
items.summary: The solicitation states that these gaps restrict NASA from simply choosing currently available COTS sensors for a lunar-gravity combustion experiment or a fire detection system in which particle properties and concentrations may not be fully known.
items.scope_notes: Applies to COTS sensor selection for lunar-g combustion experiments and fire detection systems; does not quantify the gap.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 2)
items.anchor_quote: The ISS smoke detector represents the state of the art (SOA) for spacecraft fire detection.
items.summary: The solicitation identifies the ISS smoke detector as the state of the art for spacecraft fire detection and describes it as a forward-light-scattering detector.
items.scope_notes: Detector identification only. The text does not name the detector model, does not mention SAME or any flight experiment, and gives no sensitivity data.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 2)
items.anchor_quote: subject to frequent false alarms due to the overlap of smoke particle and nuisance dust
items.summary: The ISS smoke detector is described as subject to frequent false alarms because smoke particles and nuisance dust particles have overlapping properties.
items.scope_notes: FALSE alarm (alarm without fire, from nuisance dust), not a missed alarm. "Frequent" is not quantified (no alarm counts, rates or dates) and no reference is attached to the claim in the text. Applies to the ISS forward-light-scattering smoke detector only.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 2)
items.anchor_quote: False alarms are avoided on the ISS by turning off smoke detectors during dust-generating activities
items.summary: On the ISS, false alarms are avoided by switching smoke detectors off during dust-generating activities, with vacuuming given as an example.
items.scope_notes: Operational workaround for FALSE alarms. The text does not say how often or how long detectors are off, nor does it discuss fire-detection coverage during those periods; any inference about reduced coverage is the reader's, not the solicitation's.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 2)
items.anchor_quote: a sensor system integrating multiple orthogonal properties is desired to positively identify early fires
items.summary: Because potential spacecraft smoke and nuisance pollutants vary widely in properties (both particulate and gas phase), NASA states it wants a sensor system that combines multiple orthogonal properties so that early fires are positively identified while false alarms from nuisance airborne pollutants are avoided.
items.scope_notes: Desire for multi-property (orthogonal) sensing to separate fire signatures from nuisance aerosols; no specific property set is prescribed here (the hardware list on PDF p. 258 gives particle mass, number, size and charge plus optional gas-phase parameters).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 3)
items.anchor_quote: mass of the instrument (83 lbs) prohibits its use in a spacecraft.
items.summary: The current state of the art for scientific reference-quality particle mass concentration measurement is the tapered element oscillating microbalance (TEOM; Thermo Fisher Scientific), whose footprint (43.2 x 48.3 x 139.7 cm) and 83 lb mass rule it out for spacecraft use.
items.detector: tapered element oscillating microbalance (TEOM; Thermo Fisher Scientific)

numbers.meaning: TEOM footprint dimension
TEOM footprint dimension
TEOM footprint dimension
TEOM instrument mass

items.scope_notes: Reference-quality laboratory instrument, not a fire detector; size/mass values as printed (lbs not converted by source).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 3)
items.anchor_quote: also features a physical footprint prohibitive to space flight
items.summary: The Electrical Low Pressure Impactor (ELPI; Dekati) is cited as a reference-quality instrument giving 1-10 s time-resolved particle number and charge concentrations across 6 nm to 10 um, but its footprint (40.7 x 45.4 x 24.2 cm and 48.5 lbs, excluding the specialised vacuum pump) is too large for spaceflight.
items.detector: Electrical Low Pressure Impactor (ELPI; Dekati Technologies)

numbers.meaning: lower end of ELPI time resolution
upper end of ELPI time resolution
lower end of ELPI particle size range
upper end of ELPI particle size range
ELPI footprint dimension
ELPI footprint dimension
ELPI footprint dimension
ELPI mass, not including the vacuum pump

items.scope_notes: Reference-quality laboratory instrument, not a fire detector; mass excludes the vacuum pump per the text. "um" printed as such (micrometre).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 4)
items.anchor_quote: light scattering techniques that do not detect particles smaller than ~300 nm
items.summary: Other commercial aerosol devices such as optical aerosol counters either require assumptions about particle properties (e.g., density) or have a limited range because of scattering physics; the example given is light-scattering techniques that do not detect particles smaller than approximately 300 nm.
items.detector: optical aerosol counters / light scattering techniques (generic)

numbers.meaning: approximate lower size limit below which light-scattering techniques do not detect particles

items.scope_notes: Generic statement about light-scattering aerosol instruments; the text does NOT explicitly apply the ~300 nm limit to the ISS smoke detector or to any named flight detector, and no reference is attached. Keep the approximation (~300 nm).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 4)
items.anchor_quote: Most reference-quality instruments available commercially have limited applicability at pressures below Earth ambient.
items.summary: Most commercially available reference-quality aerosol instruments have limited applicability at pressures below Earth ambient.
items.scope_notes: Qualitative; no pressure values or instrument list given. Relevant to reduced-pressure habitats (see H3.13 8.2 psia items for exploration cabin pressure, different subtopic).

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (paragraph 4)
items.anchor_quote: while maintaining a low physical footprint to enable inclusion in future combustion experiment rigs
items.summary: NASA states a need for technologies that close one or more of these measurement gaps while keeping a small physical footprint, so they can be built into future combustion experiment rigs and/or a future fire detection sensor network.
items.scope_notes: Summary need statement of the SoA section.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Civil Space Shortfall Ranking
items.anchor_quote: [Ranked 10th] ID 1520: Fire Safety for Habitation
items.summary: The fire detection scope is tied to Civil Space Shortfall ID 1520 "Fire Safety for Habitation", ranked 10th.

numbers.meaning: Civil Space Shortfall ranking of ID 1520 Fire Safety for Habitation

items.scope_notes: Same shortfall (ID 1520, 10th) is also cited by H3.13 (PDF pp. 106-107), there with a 2024 Integrated Ranking attribution.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > Relevance / Science Traceability
items.anchor_quote: including potential follow-ons to the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) lunar lander payload
items.summary: The scope supports fundamental combustion science under the 2023 BPS Decadal Survey theme on phenomena hidden by gravity (KSQ #10) and BPS combustion experiments, including possible follow-ons to the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) lunar lander payload; it may also interest the Mars Campaign Office for Spacecraft Fire Safety experiments and Life Support Systems particulate-monitoring flight demonstrations.
items.scope_notes: Programmatic traceability; FM2 and Spacecraft Fire Safety experiments are named but no results from them are given.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > References, item 1
items.anchor_quote: Pyrolysis Smoke Generated Under Low-Gravity Conditions,
items.summary: Reference 1 of the fire detection scope: Mulholland, Meyer, Urban, Ruff, Yuan, Bryg, Cleary, Yang, "Pyrolysis Smoke Generated Under Low-Gravity Conditions," Aerosol Science and Technology 2015, vol. 49, issue 5, pp. 310-321, doi 10.1080/02786826.2015.1025125.
items.scope_notes: Citation only; the solicitation does not summarise this paper's results.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > References, item 2
items.anchor_quote: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment,
items.summary: Reference 2 of the fire detection scope: Meyer, Urban, Mulholland, Bryg, Yuan, Ruff, Cleary, Yang, "Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment," Fire Safety Journal 2018, vol. 98, pp. 74-81, doi 10.1016/j.firesaf.2018.04.004.
items.scope_notes: Citation only; the solicitation does not summarise this paper's results and does not list author affiliations.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > References, item 3
items.anchor_quote: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters,
items.summary: Reference 3 of the fire detection scope: Urban, Dietrich, Brooker, Meyer, Ruff, "Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters," ICES 2016, NTRS 20170000248. References 4-5 are the 2023-2032 BPS Decadal Survey and the NASA Civil Space Shortfalls page.
items.scope_notes: Citation only; no findings summarised in the solicitation.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 2 "Fire Detection Sensing for Space Research" > State of the Art and Critical Gaps (absence check over full S15.03 text, PDF pp. 254-260, and whole document)
items.anchor_quote: The ISS smoke detector represents the state of the art (SOA) for spacecraft fire detection.
items.summary: Mentions SAME? NO. The S15.03 text discusses the ISS smoke detector and cites low-gravity smoke papers but never names SAME or the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment; a case-sensitive whole-word search for "SAME" and a search for "Smoke Aerosol" return 0 hits in the entire 456-page document (also 0 hits for DAFT and ACME).
items.scope_notes: Absence holds for this document only (text extracted with pdftotext); it is not evidence about NASA's research record.

items.location: S16.07 Cryogenic Systems for Sensors and Detectors > References (only Kapton hit in the document)
items.anchor_quote: Thermal Properties of Double-Aluminized Kapton at Low Temperatures
items.summary: Mentions Kapton? NO within S15.03. The only occurrence of "Kapton" in the whole document is a reference title on cryogenic thermal properties of double-aluminized Kapton in subtopic S16.07 (PDF p. 282), unrelated to fire detection.
items.scope_notes: Whole-document search (case-insensitive) for "Kapton": 1 hit, on PDF p. 282.

items.location: S15.03 Scope 2 references (absence check over S15.03 and whole document)
items.anchor_quote: Pyrolysis Smoke Generated Under Low-Gravity Conditions,
items.summary: Mentions Teflon? NO. "Teflon", "PTFE" and "polytetrafluoroethylene" return 0 hits in the whole document; the fire detection scope names no smoke-source materials at all (only an unrelated "Ag/FEP thermal control surfaces" reference title appears in Z-LIVE.02, PDF p. 344).
items.scope_notes: Absence holds for this document only.

items.location: S15.03 Scope 2 references (check for 2018 NASA/NIST findings)
items.anchor_quote: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment,
items.summary: Mentions the 2018 NASA/NIST findings? PARTIAL / CITATION ONLY. S15.03 lists the 2018 Fire Safety Journal paper by Meyer et al. (and the 2015 Aerosol Science and Technology paper) as references 1-2, but the scope text neither summarises their findings nor names NIST or any author affiliation, and the SoA statements (frequent false alarms, ~300 nm light-scattering limit, a priori knowledge requirement) carry no in-text reference markers. Whole-word "NIST" appears only on PDF p. 19 (a FIPS 201-3 URL) and p. 180 (S11.04, NIST-made detector readout arrays), both unrelated to fire.
items.scope_notes: Do not attribute specific SoA statements to the 2018 paper on the basis of this solicitation alone; that link would need the paper itself.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 1 "Continuous Environmental Sensing to Monitor the Space-Built Environment and Its Microbiome" > hardware requirements (PDF pp. 254-257)
items.anchor_quote: volatile organic compounds, particulate concentrations, and light.
items.summary: Scope 1 of S15.03 (PDF pp. 254-257) seeks continuous, highly automated biomonitoring and physico-chemical monitoring of space habitats; particulate concentrations are listed among example environmental variables (with humidity, temperature, radiation, vibration, major/trace gases, VOCs and light). Hardware should work across habitat environments (non-standard atmosphere, pressure, airflow, gravity), with buffer storage for at least a few weeks desired; expected TRL 3 to 5.
items.scope_notes: Habitat environmental/microbiome monitoring scope; particulate concentration is one optional variable. Not a fire detection scope.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 1 > State of the Art and Critical Gaps
items.anchor_quote: Consistent monitoring is labor-intensive and captures only some kinds of relevant data
items.summary: Scope 1 SoA notes that ISS habitat-level data streams (e.g., radiation, temperature, humidity) are often not at the temporal/spatial scale relevant to plant and microbial health, that consistent monitoring is labour-intensive and partial, and that the most recent quantification of airborne microbial particulates on the ISS cited is a 2006 publication.

numbers.meaning: publication year of the most recent cited quantification of ISS airborne microbial particulates

items.scope_notes: About airborne microbial particulates and habitat monitoring, not smoke detection.

items.location: S15.03 > Scope 1 > State of the Art and Critical Gaps
items.anchor_quote: Much of this technology can be prohibitively large and is not compatible with microgravity
items.summary: Commercial continuous-monitoring tools exist for ground labs (e.g., particle size analyzers, some able to measure biofluorescent particles, used in clean rooms), but much of this technology is prohibitively large and not compatible with microgravity, partial gravity or unusual atmospheric pressures. The scope cites Civil Space Shortfall ID 1519 Environmental Monitoring for Habitation (ranked 7th).
items.detector: commercial particle size analyzers (incl. biofluorescent particle capable)

numbers.meaning: Civil Space Shortfall ranking of ID 1519 Environmental Monitoring for Habitation

items.scope_notes: Applies to commercial particle size analyzers in general (scope 1); no specific instrument or values given.

items.location: S17.03 Fault Management Technologies (Lead GRC; participating ARC, JPL, MSFC; PDF pp. 303-308) > excluded areas
items.anchor_quote: Fault management technologies as a specific component to environmental monitoring (including fire
items.summary: Subtopic S17.03 excludes fault management technologies that are a specific component of environmental monitoring, including fire detection, and directs such proposals to S15.03.
items.scope_notes: Confirms S15.03 is the designated home for fire detection proposals within this solicitation.

items.location: H3.13 subtopic header (PDF pp. 104-107; printed pp. 96-99)
items.anchor_quote: H3.13: Oxygen Compatible Habitation Solutions for Exploration
items.summary: Subtopic H3.13 "Oxygen Compatible Habitation Solutions for Exploration Environments (SBIR)" (ESDMD/SOMD) is led by MSFC with ARC, GRC, JSC, KSC and LaRC participating; PDF pages 104-107. Scopes: "Oxygen Compatible Materials" (PDF pp. 105-106) and "Alternative Approaches to Habitation and Logistic Challenges in High Oxygen Environments" (PDF pp. 106-107).
items.scope_notes: Fire-safety (material flammability) subtopic, not fire detection; included because it gives numeric exploration-cabin atmosphere conditions relevant to where detectors must work.

items.location: H3.13 > Subtopic Introduction
items.anchor_quote: The targeted nominal environment for exploration missions is 8.2 psia cabin pressure and >33.7
items.summary: Exploration missions with frequent EVAs benefit from a lower-than-ambient cabin pressure to shorten prebreathe, which requires higher O2 concentration; the targeted nominal environment is 8.2 psia and more than 33.7 vol% O2 (balance nitrogen), and because of control-system limitations O2 may reach as high as 38 vol%, increasing flammability risk.

numbers.meaning: targeted nominal exploration cabin pressure
targeted nominal oxygen concentration (greater than)
possible maximum O2 concentration due to control-system limitations

items.scope_notes: Exploration cabin atmosphere design values (not a test). pressure_kpa is the extractor's conversion of 8.2 psia (x 6.894757 = 56.5 kPa), not printed in the source; atmosphere_o2_vol_pct = nominal lower bound (>33.7), with up to 38 vol% possible.

items.location: H3.13 > Subtopic Introduction
items.anchor_quote: particularly challenging for lunar surface missions where partial gravity further exacerbates the risk
items.summary: The increased flammability risk at elevated O2 is described as especially challenging for lunar surface missions, where partial gravity further worsens the risk.
items.scope_notes: Qualitative statement about flammability risk (materials), not detection; no data given.

items.location: H3.13 > Subtopic Introduction
items.anchor_quote: Foams used on the International Space Station (ISS) have only been tested to 30% O2
items.summary: Foams used on the ISS have only been tested up to 30% O2 and, in that testing, burned beyond the 6-inch limit (C rating); other life support and habitation materials have similar issues. Plastic storage bags are said to produce molten drips that can ignite other materials.

numbers.meaning: highest O2 level to which ISS foams have been tested
burn-length limit exceeded in testing (C rating)

items.location: H3.13 > Subtopic Introduction / Scope "Oxygen Compatible Materials"
items.anchor_quote: There are very few known materials that are non-flammable at 38% oxygen,
items.summary: Very few known materials are non-flammable at 38% oxygen, so new materials are needed that pass NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 Upward Flame Propagation at 38 vol% O2 (e.g., upholstery fabrics, crew restraints, acoustic barriers, insulation, storage/packaging materials, foams). Expected TRL 3 to 5.

items.location: H3.13 > Scope "Alternative Approaches to Habitation and Logistic Challenges in High Oxygen Environments"
items.anchor_quote: this is not a call for new materials, but rather a call for new techniques
items.summary: For habitats at 8.2 psia and 33.7% oxygen, where most known materials are highly flammable, the second H3.13 scope seeks alternative techniques that avoid flammable materials (e.g., for food packaging, trash containment, tape, labels, clothing dryers/hampers, restraints) rather than new materials. Expected TRL 3 to 6.

open_questions: Which instrument/data underlie the solicitation's statements that the ISS forward-light-scattering smoke detector has 'frequent' false alarms and that light-scattering techniques miss particles below ~300 nm? The S15.03 text gives no in-text reference markers; the cited 2015/2018 low-gravity smoke papers would need to be checked directly.

How often and for how long are ISS smoke detectors switched off during dust-generating activities (e.g., vacuuming)? The solicitation states the practice but gives no frequency, duration, or coverage analysis.

The solicitation asks for 10-300 nm particle coverage and >1 mg/m3 capability but gives no lower concentration threshold or alarm criterion for a 'slow-moving spacecraft fire'; what concentration/size targets does NASA use for alarm sensitivity?

Reduced-pressure / elevated-O2 operation is required qualitatively in S15.03; the only numeric exploration-atmosphere values in this document (8.2 psia, >33.7 vol% O2, up to 38 vol%) come from H3.13, a materials subtopic. Are these the target detector test conditions?
SBIR Phase I awards made under S15.03 scope 2 (FY2025) were not examined; whether any selected proposal addresses multi-parameter (orthogonal) smoke sensing is unknown within the examined source.
The solicitation's SF-30 dates the solicitation 1/08/2025 while Section 1.2 states release on January 7, 2025; the discrepancy is unresolved (administrative only).
